arthur-neill-vinegar-bend-1910-08-22.A2:
NEGRO MAKES CONFESSION TELLS OF ATTACK ON WOMAN AT AXIS. Declares He is Not Responsible for Murder of Negro, However— Taken to Mobile for Safe-Kepeling,
Mobile, Aug. 22.—(Special.)—Arthur Neill, a negro, committed rape on Mrs. J. O. Gibson, at Axis, this county, according to a confession alleged to have been made by him yesterday at Vinegar Bend, Washington County, in the stockades where he was sent from this county to serve a sentence for vagrancy, having been arrested shortly after the horrible crime was committed at Axis, and sent here after being given trial by Justice Anderson and sent to Vinegar Bend for ninety days at hard labor.

Neill is said to have made the confession to Warden Miller, in charge of the Vinegar Bend stockade, yesterday after it was discovered that his underclothing, which he had failed to remove since his incarceration there, was covered with blood.

Neill is said to have stated to Warder Miller that he raped Mrs. Gibson, but that Bill Walker was the man who killed Jesse Brown with a rifle taken from the Gibson home by Neill after he had accomplished his crime on Mrs. Gibson.

When Neill was ordered to disrobe in order that he could don stripes at the stockade, it was discovered that his clothes were covered with blood. He then made free and full confession.

Deputy Sheriff Wade and two other deputies were notified by the warden of the negro's confession, and they left for Vinegar Bend this morning. On arrival there, the negro repeated to them the confession he had made to Warden Miller.

When it became known at Vinegar Bend that the confession had been made there was great excitement in the village, and there was strong talk of a lynching. President N. E. Turner of the Vinegar Bend Lumber Company, who owns the stockade, used his best persuasion and succeeded in calming the irate citizens and the negro was allowed to be placed on a freight train and brought to Mobile by Deputy Wade and his assistants.

President Turner of the Vinegar Bend Company, after consultation with Warden Miller and the deputies from Mobile County, decided that the stockade was not sufficiently strong to protect the negro in event of an attempt at mob violence, hence the transfer of the prisoner to Mobile County. Neill was brought to Mobile on a freight train at 6:25 o'clock and placed in jail. The transfer of the negro from the train to an electric car, thence to the jail, was without undue excitement.
arthur-neill-vinegar-bend-1910-08-22.A3:
TO AN UGLY CRIME
ADMITS HE IS THE ASSAILANT OF MRS. GIBSON—IS RUSHED TO THE MOBILE JAIL TO AVOID A LYNCHING
Mobile, August 22.—(Special.)—Arthur Neill, a negro recently sent to the stockade at Vinegar Bend for vagrancy, yesterday confessed to a warden and later to Mobile deputies that he assaulted Mrs. J. O. Gibson, cut her with a knife and also slashed her young brother on the morning of July 31. The confession was carefully guarded until this afternoon when Mobile deputies, seeing a mob forming, brought the negro to this city on a through freight train. When the negro was ordered to disrobe at the stockade to put on convict stripes blood was discovered on his clothing. This he could not explain and was forced to confess.

Gus Walker some time ago was arrested at Benndale, Miss., for the crime against Mrs. Gibson. The negro was brought to Mobile and closely guarded in the county jail to prevent a lynching. Walker admitted killing a negro and stealing the latter's wife but strongly maintained his innocence of assailing Mrs. Gibson.

Two days after Walker's arrest Mrs. Gibson, accompanied by her husband, called at the Mobile jail and identified Walker as her assailant. Her identification at the time was considered positive in that she picked Walker out from a bunch of negro prisoners and pointing at the black said, "That's the man." She was positive that she was right at the time.

Citizens of Vinegar Bend upon hearing of Neill's confession were thrown into great excitement and there was strong talk of lynching.

This afternoon according to the deputies the lynching bee was so busy at Vinegar Bend the Mobile deputies had the agent flag a fast freight train, placed the negro Neill abroad and reached Mobile shortly after 6 o'clock. News of the nego's confession did not become known here until the arrival of the negro.

There is some excitement here that may become serious later tonight.
arthur-neill-vinegar-bend-1910-08-22.A4:
NEGRO CONFESSES TO SECOND CRIME
Mobile, August 24.—(Special.)—Arthur McNeill, alias Neill, confessed assailant of Mrs. J. O. Gibson of Axis, today confessed to having committed a similar offense six years ago against a white woman of Pine Hill named Alice Davis.

He made his confession to Chief Jailer A. Wade and it was voluntary on the part of the negro. "I want to tell everything," said McNeill to Jailer Wade this morning. "I am in trouble but am calm and I want to get the whole business off my mind."

McNeill said his relatives live on the Clay Sheffield plantation, six miles from Pine Hill, and he has a father, mother, sister and two brothers. After committing the crime at Pine Hill McNeill said he fled but has returned several times, the last of which was about a month ago. He worked at the Mobile and Ohio railroad round house in Mobile about a month before going to Axis, where he committed the crime against Mrs. Gibson.

Jailer Wade has written Clay Sheffield at Pine Hill and also to the sheriff of Wilcox county asking them for further particulars concerning the negro and to substantiate McNeill's confession regarding the Davis woman. A special grand jury is being summoned to meet here August 31 to try McNeill and Bill Walker. The latter for murder and assault committed at the time of the Axis crime done by McNeill.
arthur-neill-vinegar-bend-1910-08-22.A5:
NEGRO'S STORY IS PROVEN FALSE
WHICH DID NOT OCCUR—THE
GULF CITY WILL HAVE AN AERO
CLUB
Mobile, August 25.—(Special.)—Investigation into the second confession of Arthur McNeill, the negro held here for criminally assaulting Mrs. J. O. Gibson at Axis last July, that he had also assaulted Alice Davis, a white woman, near Pinehill six years ago, disproves the negro's story. The woman McNeill confesses to have assaulted has been dead for eight years, according to her father, Amos Davis, a farmer of near Pinehill. Pinehill is McNeill's home and his relatives reside there. Persons acquainted with the negro say he often told stories that proved false after investigation. Mrs. J. O. Gibson of Axis has been asked to come to Mobile to look at McNeill, who at the Vinegar Bend stockade last Sunday confessed to having committed the crime for which another negro, Bill Walker, had been arrested and held.

arthur-neill-vinegar-bend-1910-08-22.A8:
NEGRO CRIMINAL
WILL BE HANGED
Mobile, September 8.—(Special.)—The Axis assault and murder cases terminated today in the city court here when Bill Walker, alias Cooney Ford, a negro, was tried on the charge of murder and sentenced to death by a jury that took only 10 minutes to deliberate. Receiving this verdict the prosecutor asked the court that the assault cases not be tried, as the law was satisfied with hanging Walker for murdering a negro, Jesse Brown, July 31, the same night of the assault. It is learned today that the reason the special grand jury did not hold Arthur McNeill, who confessed to assaulting Mrs. J. O. Gibson, was that McNeill is crazy and had been so persistently questioned by officers that he weakened and confessed though innocent. Walker, though denying the crime, was held for the attack on the woman.

It is believed that the negro who attacked Miss Frances Williams near Whistle last night, but was frightened away and pursued all night and all today by posses of citizens, has escaped. Many members of the posse have returned home and excitement caused by the attack has subsided. Should the negro be caught in the neighborhood he will be summarily dealt with.

clara-bladus-buckner-1910-08-05.A1:
VENGEFUL MOB IS SEEKING FOR NEGRO
Kansas City, Aug. 5.—Armed with guns and clubs a mob is hunting a negro in the brush near Buckner, Mo. The negro is accused of attacking Clara Bladus, aged 15, daughter of a farmer. The mob threatens to burn him. Another negro was captured and spirited away by the authorities. It is reported the two negroes attacked the girl.
clara-bladus-buckner-1910-08-05.A5:
GIRL ATTACKED IN HER HOME
Daughter of Farmer Near Kansas City Assaulted by Unidentified Man.
INDEPENDENCE, Mo., Aug. 5.—Clara Baldus, the 16-year-old daughter of Joseph Baldus, a farmer living nine miles east of this city, while alone in her home today was attacked by a man, chloroformed and bound to a chair. The man fled, leaving her unconscious.

Other members of the Baldus family had gone to Kansas City shopping. The girl was at work in the kitchen when she heard a step behind her. Before she could look around, she was bound, blindfolded and gagged. Then she became unconscious. When she recovered an hour later, she was alone, fastened to a chair in another room. She could not tell the police whether her assailant was a negro.

Her condition is not dangerous.
clara-bladus-buckner-1910-08-05.A6:
MOB WITH GUNS
HUNTING FIEND
Negro Attack Young Girl and
Makes His Escape Into
Brush.
KANSAS CITY, MO., August 6.—A mob of men with clubs and guns and hunting a negro in the brush near Buckner, Mo., threatening to burn him at the stake for an attack to-day on Clara Baldus, 15 year-old daughter of a farmer near Independence. Another negro has been captured and spirited away by officials.
clara-bladus-buckner-1910-08-05.A10:
YOUNG WOMAN
DRUGGED AND TIED
While Family Was Absent She Was Chloroformed and Tied to Chair
Kansas City, Aug. 8.—As Clara Baldus, 16 years old, was bending over a gasoline stove to light it in her home on a farm nine miles east of Independence at 9 o'clock this morning she heard footsteps behind her. Before she could turn a hand seized her throat, a wad of cotton was thrust in her mouth and a handkerchief was tied around her face. Then she lost consciousness.

When the girl recovered, nearly an hour later, she was in the dining room, tied to a chair. Her lips were slightly burned and the air of the room was heavy with the odor of chloroform. She freed herself and staggered to the telephone to call the police of Independence. Then she became unconscious again.

All Alone in the House.

The Baldus home is nine miles east of Independence on the Daniel Mason farm. Joseph Baldus, the father, his wife and Cora Baldus, a sister, 19 years old, left early this morning in a wagon for Kansas City. They had planned to spend the day here shopping. Clara remained at home and had intended to do some ironing. It was nearly an hour after the family left when she went to the kitchen to light the gasoline stove.

Miss Baldus got some matches off a shelf in the kitchen and then turned to the stove. Then she heard the footsteps and the attack followed. To W. W. Twyman, a deputy constable, who with other officers went to the Baldus home, she gave this version of the attack:

Heard Footsteps.

"It was all quiet. I was all alone. But I was not afraid as I have been left alone often on the place. I struck a match to light the stove. Then I heard the footsteps behind me. The next thing I knew someone had seized me and put some cotton in my mouth.

"Then he tried to tie a handkerchief around my mouth and I lost consciousness. I can remember waking up once in the dining room and being tied to a chair. Then I went back to sleep again. It was nearly 10 o'clock before I came to, got loose and telephoned to Independence for the officers."

Two Negroes Questioned.

Miss Baldus said she did not see the man who attacked her. When the alarm was given, the entire neighborhood turned out to search for the assailant. Two negroes were found hiding in a cornfield on Joseph Webb's farm, a half mile away. They were questioned by the officers, but, as there was no evidence on which to hold them, they were released.

The motive for the attack is a mystery. Miss Baldus says she was not injured except by the drug and the tying. Nothing is missing from the farm.

With Revolver, Mask and Gag.

Miss Baldus told the officers she had seen a strange man with a revolver, a mask and a gag, near her home two weeks ago. She paid no attention, she said.

The girl told the officers she had no suitors.

A neighborhood posse of one hundred men, most of them recruited from a stone quarry near the Baldus
A Mystery to the Parents.
The motive for the attack was a mystery concerning which the parents would not venture a guess this afternoon. Mr. and Mrs. Baldus, accompanied by their daughter, Cora, reached Independence at 4 o'clock on their way to their home. They had heard in Kansas City of the strange happening at the farm.
"I can't imagine who attacked my daughter, unless it was two men seen near our house two weeks ago," Mr. Baldus said. "These men were loitering about the premises when my daughter noticed them. One was carrying something that she took to be a mask. As soon as they saw that they were observed, they disappeared."
Joseph Baldus, the father, is a Swiss. He is the owner of a 300-acre farm where he now lives, and owns several valuable farms in Saline county, his former home.

fletcher-reeves-gadsden-1910-08-12.A2:
While on Scaffold, Condemned Negro Gives His Version of Affray and Gives Advice to His Race.
Centerville, Aug. 12.—(Special.)—Tolly Mason, a negro, who murdered Richard Meigs, a respected white citizen of Bibb County, more than a year ago, and who was convicted at a special term of the Circuit Court and whose conviction was affirmed by the Supreme Court of Alabama, was hung at noon today in the yard of the county jail.

The black cap was adjusted a few moments before noon and promptly at noon the trap was sprung. The condemned man's neck was broken, and he died without a struggle. The execution was carried to a finish without a hitch.

After mounting the scaffold of the gallows, Mason made a talk of about five minutes to the crowd which had assembled in the yard. He gave his version of the causes leading up to the killing, stating that when he first saw his victim on the morning of the killing he had no idea of doing harm to him. He stated that Meigs first abused him and started at him with a weapon.

He warned the members of his race against violating the law. He told his brother, who was in the crowd, to make his children obey and to punish them if they failed to obey, stating that he wanted his children brought up in the right way. The condemned man displayed remarkable nerve, and did not flinch in the least when the black cap was placed over his face and the noose placed about his neck.

After eleven minutes from the time the trap was sprung the attending physicians pronounced life extinct, and the body was cut down and turned over to his relatives.

When upon the scaffold, the condemned man stated that he had made his peace with God and was not afraid to die.

A large crowd came to town this morning and many persons mounted the tops of houses hoping to be able to see the scaffold. Members of the condemned man's race held religious services with him at the jail this morning, and three negro preachers were with him until the last. The crowd in town today was orderly. Seven members of the Melgs family were in Centerville.

This is the first execution in Bibb County in nearly ten years.

Huntsville, Aug. 12—(Special.)—W. W. Windham, of Moulton, who runs one of the largest general merchandise businesses in Lawrence County, has filed a petition in the bankruptcy court here asking relief from liabilities estimated at $18,164. His creditors are principally jobbers in a dozen Southern cities. Petitioner's assets, if taken at their face value, exceed the liabilities, amounting to $25,-625. including mortgages, notes, open accounts, collateral in banks, incumbered real estate and personal property which is claimed as exempt. Of the liabilities, the sum of $3,271 is secured by collateral, $4,118 is partially secured by waive notes and mortgages. $1,202 is preferred claims, while $9,672 is unsecured

Huntsville, Aug. 12—(Special.)—At a meeting in the office of Jere Murphy, Referee in Bankruptcy, the creditors of the bankrupt DeLoach Mill Manufacturing Company, of Bridgeport, Ala., elected David A. Grayson, Lawrence Brown and W. D. Scarborough as trustees. The property of the DeLoach Company is under a mortgage of $100,000 and this will consume practically all of the assets. There are liabilities of about $25,000 in addition to the mortgage that are unsecured. The bankrupt concern's big plant is being operated by the DeLoach Manufacturing Company under a lease.

Gadsden, Aug. 12—Patrolman R. L. Leath shot and killed Fletcher Reeves, a negro whiskey seller, at midnight last night. The negro was selling whiskey at a negro dance pavilion and when the officer placed him under arrest he struck the officer and attempted to take his gun from him. The negro was shot through the heart and died instantly. The negro came here from Chattanooga with a large supply of liquor and was selling it.

Headland, Aug. 12.—(Special.)—The first bale of new crop cotton was brought to Headland today by T. A. Dykes and sold to W. W. Camp and Brother at 25 cents per pound. It weighed 364 pounds and brought $91, classing about Liverpool fully mid- dling.

FINAL TRIBUTE PAID
TO MICHAEL CODY, SR

Dothan, Aug. 12.—(Special.)—The funeral of Michael Cody, Sr., was held from the First Baptist Church this morning at 10 o'clock, Rev. W. M. Anderson, of Woodlawn, officiating.

A large number of friends and relatives followed the bier to its last resting place. The body was attended by the local lodge of Masons.

Dr. C. E. Granberry, of Gordon, who died there Wednesday afternoon was buried this afternoon at the city cemetery of this place. The funeral was held from the residence of his parents on South Foster Street, at 3 o'clock, Rev. R. H. Folmar officiating.

The work of street paving is being shed as fast as is practicable. East Street has been closed from St. Andrews to the Central crossing for more than a week, and preparations now are being made to close it from St. Andrews to Foster, one of the most congested business districts of the city.

Every laborer procurable has been pressed into service, and even then they are short handed, as there are many buildings going up in the city.

Porter and Couch rapidly are completing their contract for the sidewalk paving, Oates Street having been finished, and have begun work on West Main.

The City Council has awarded a contract to a Pensacola firm for paving the remainder of the streets not included in the Porter and Couch contract.

Work is being pushed on the Federal building, although there are no visible signs of it as yet. Most of the work being done now is inside work.

There are several other large buildings going up in the business district of the city and most of them are promised to be ready for occupancy by September
fletcher-reeves-gadsden-1910-08-12.A3:
THE IDLER.
I picked up the Columbia Record of last Friday while my thoughts were on this subject and I began with the first column subject and I began with the first column on the first page and the first thing under a two column head was an account of the chase after a man named Wendling who it seems is charged with murdering Alma Kellner whose mutilated body was found in a cellar. The chase after Wendling covered 13,000 miles. Then right under this story appeared the account of a man beating his wife into a jelly with a hammer. Then the Oklahoma investigation frauds. Then an account of the Yarborough case right here in Newberry. A man was killed by the side of a woman without warning by the woman's husband. At the same place, Hot Springs, Ark., at the same time a man was shot to death while sitting in front of a grocery store. Then follows the account of Mayor Gaynor's condition and following that the suicide of a man at Winston-Salem. A baseball player took a shower bath after a game and dies. Then appears some resolutions of a Baptist Association in Abbeville condemning the State, which are not filled with the Christian spirit nor do they breathe the atmosphere of temperance, or justice, or fairness. A patrolman in Alabama slays a negro. Thugs in New York rob a well to do resident of Harlem and throw him into North river. Four young negroes in Columbia release a freight car and the result is a costly smash-up. A small negro boy in Columbia is run over by a motor cycle. A soldier on the way to the encampment at Aiken threw a rock from the train at a negro workman which will probably cause the loss of an eye. There may be other crimes in this same paper. Frequently the list is much longer but this is a pretty good list for one afternoon paper. And the Recorder's court in Columbia was not reported in detail.

Is this evidence that the world is growing better? Is this good food for the soul? I don't know much about the newspaper business and I reckon it is right to publish all this sort of stuff but really I can't see anything helpful or uplifting to the people in reading about all these crimes.
Resolved, That the sunrise with its glorious effulgence of light and color, with its awakening of bird's songs and busy life means another day has come. Another day means another chance. A chance to forget yesterday and commence all over again. Forgive yourself and others for the mistakes of yesterday and resolve that today you'll be on time like the sun

keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A2:
ON TRAIL OF NEGROES
Three Lynchings We'll Follow Their Capture.
Three Lynchings Will Follow Their Capture.

Mobile, Ala., August 17.—With a triple lynching almost certain to follow their capture, armed citizens of Bay Minnette, Ala., a small town east of Mobile, are pursuing three negroes who to-night shot and killed Town Marshal Joseph Smith. Bloodhounds and officers were sent from Mobile to assist in the search.

On the request of a white woman, in front of whose honour the three negroes—turpentine hands—were loitering, Smith went to the scene to arrest the negroes. Two of the negroes opened fire when the officer appeared, Smith being instantly killed.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A3:
SCOUR BALDWIN FOR BLACK PAIR Hundreds of Armed Men Follow Dogs. MAY BE ESCAPED PRISONERS Marshal Smith's Slayers Still Elude Posses. BELIEVED THAT TWO NEGROES ESCAPED FROM CONECUH COUN- TY JAIL—BRAVE OFFICER IS BURIED WITH HONORS.
Bay Minette, Aug. 18—(Special.)—An angry mob still is scouring the woods in this vicinity for the negro who shot and instantly killed Town Marshal Joseph W. Smith last night at 6:15 o'clock. The mob is being organized and it is thought that the efforts of the men who have made search for the negro will be rewarded by effecting the capture soon. Hounds from Brewton and Mobile have been placed in the woods and are on the trail.

The negro who shot Smith was about 5 feet 11 inches tall and had been working recently at some turpentine still. He was in comptny with a smaller negro and both escaped to the woods after the shooting.

Smith heard of their being in town when they sent Bob Morgan for a team to go to another still a short distance from here. They were refused a team. Smith had been watching for the negroes who escaped from Evergreen, and since these refused to come into town, he lost no time in going to the place where they were, a short distance back of the Louisville and Nashville depot.

When he arrived there, he began questioning them and when they recognized that he was an official, the larger one pulled his revolver of 38 calibre and shot at Smith four times in quick succession. The first shot entered just above the heart and the second grazed his side and entered his arm. He fell forward instantly, crushing his skull on the track. The killing was witnessed by several women living in that vicinity and the alarm was sent out. The two negroes fled immediately.

Posses Soon Form.

Soon word had reached town and in a very short time fully 250 men were in the woods with their arms searching for the negroes. Bob Morgan who was at the depot at the time of the shooting was held and gave out the descriptions of the other two. He stated that he had come from Atmore with the two negroes and that he did not know their full names, though he knew the last name of the large negro who did the killing to be Keyser, and thought his first name to be Aaron. The smalled negro was called Sidney.

The trail was followed from the place of the shooting over a hill where the small negro lost his left shoe. The trail led into the woods where it was lost until this morning. The hounds from Mobile have been taken to Daphne and will work back from that place while the hounds

from Brewton were kept on the trail all night. Sheriff Fountain of Brewton is with the dogs which belong to the Cedar Creek Mill Company, and Deputy Sheriff J. H. McKenzie of Mobile and F. S. Stone are with the dogs on the Daphne road.

During the night, word was sent to Dyas where about fifty men kept watch and also at Hurricane where the same number were on guard. Deputy Sheriff McGill and Dave Walton captured a negro on an outgoing train near Dyas and he is now in the local jail. The crowd at the depot here last night took another from the train here who may be one who escaped from the jail at Evergreen. He too is in the jail. Word was received from Atmore that a negro and a white man had been taken from the train there but the negro did not answer the description sent.

Cannot Enter Jail.

Rob Morgan is known to be innocent and probably will be released. It is impossible to enter the jail today as the keys which were held by the marshal at the time he was killed. were taken into the woods by one of the first to reach him and the jail cannot be entered. The local sheriff also is in the woods with the other set of keys.

Yesterday afternoon Section Foreman Stevens offered the two negroes work, but both of them showed signs of timidity in close range and stated that they wanted turpentine work. It is not improbable that they are the ones who escaped from Evergreen.

All the men who are searching for the negroes are armed to the teeth and it is certain that they will be riddled with bullets if seen.

The death of Marshal Smith removes one of the most diligent and fearless officers Bay Minette ever has known. He was buried this afternoon at 3 o'clock from his residence, the funeral being in charge of the Masonic Lodge of this place, of which organization, he was a member. He leaves a wife and two grown daughters. He has been serving as Town Marshal and Deputy Sheriff for about ten years.

A heavy rain fell in this vicinity shortly after dinner today, and the trail being followed as that taken by the negro who killed Marshal Smith last night was lost completely. The rain was accompanied by a driving wind.

The posses are being organized and a systematic effort is being made to capture the murderer. By 6 o'clock this evening most of the men had come in and were organizing for a complete search. A new set of dogs has been brought here and these will take up the trail at once.

The trail which was lost during the rain indicated that the negroes were headed for Gateswood, from which place they probably intend going to Pensacola. All authorities throughout the surrounding counties have been notified and a complete description has been sent out.

Word received here at 7:40 o'clock from Hurricane is that two negroes answering well the description sent out had been captured at that place.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A6:
POSSE STILL SEEKING
FUGITIVE NEGROES.
Pensacola, Fla., August 21. After tramping fifty miles across the swamps of Baldwin county, Alabama, twenty members of a posse which set out from Bay Mine several days ago bent upon capturing and lynching three negroes who shot and killed Marshal White, of that place, last Tuesday, reached Pensacola late today, just a few hours behind one of the negroes wanted. Oscar Moore, who was arrested by the police shortly after noon, was promptly identified by the Baldwin county men as one of the alleged murderers. Feeling among the possemen against the negro was high, but there was no talk of attempting to harm him here, and it was announced that the men would leave at midnight to continue to search for the two other negroes.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A9:
EIGHTEEN LOSE LIVES. London, Aug. 22.—Eighteen lives were lost when the British cruiser Redford ran ashore on the rocks of Quedpart Island, Korea, yesterday, according to the report received here by the admirality. The men were members of the engine room staff. Two Men Hold up Steamer at Sea and Shoot the Captain Keyser Brown Caught at the Earnest Turpentine Camps by a Posse NEGRO ADMITS BEING PRESENT WHEN THE BAY MINETTE OF- FICER WAS KILLED, BUT CLAIMS THE OTHER MAN DID IT—BROWN HAD BEEN SHOT, EVIDENTLY BY ANOTHER POSSE.
Keyser Brown, the negro wanted for shooting Marshal Smith to death at Bay Minette, Ala., last Wednesday, was arrested yesterday morning by Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews at the turpentine camp of W. T. Earnest near Muscogee, Andrews being accompanied by about 15 men from Bay Minette who since Saturday night have been scouring the country round about Muscogee for Brown and another negro, Sidney Hunter, who was supposed to be with him when he killed the town marshal at Bay Minette.

The arrest is the result of splendid work on the part of Chief of Police Frank Sanders and J. B. Graham, a government prisoner, and Sneriff Van Pelt. A good description of the men wanted was handed the chief from The Journal office Saturday night. The chief knew that Graham was an old turpentine operator and that he had large experience with negroes. He showed him the description. Graham at once identified the men as Keyser Brown and Sidney Hunter and added so much to the descriptions that a capture was almost certain. He also told that Brown was wanted for shooting another negro and that he was liable to be in the vicinity of Muscogee, or possibly about Flomaton. Chief Sanders sent a good man with Sheriff Van Pelt who went out in an automobile and not only searched for the negroes but notified outlying deputies and deputized other men liable to find the negroes.

Yesterday morning Andrews led the posse to an old shack where the negro was found asleep. Andrews jumped straddle of him and handcuffed him. The negro admitted he was with Hunter when the shooting occurred at Bay minette but claimed Hunter did the shooting. He directed the officers to go to Flomaton and find the negro Hunter. It was found that the negro had been shot, probably by a searching party in the side and back, one bullet making a bad wound. The other wound was one made with a charge of bird shot. Sheriff Boyd of Bay Minette says Brown is the right negro without a doubt. Brown was brought to Pensacola last night and located in the county jail. There is a reward outstanding for him of $200. The search for Hunter is still going on and Sheriff Van Pelt hopes to land him some time today.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A10:
Are Suspected of Being Men Who Attacked Mrs. Middleton Sunday Night. LATER WENT TO THE HOME OF FLOYD KETTRELL, BUT WERE DRIVEN AWAY BY MISS LENA BOWMAN AT THE POINT OF A REVOLVER, WHO FURNISHED THE DESCRIPTION BY WHICH THE NEGROES WERE CAPTUR-ED—MRS. MIDDLETON WAS NOT INJURED.
Suspected of being the parties who Sunday night attempted to criminally assault Mrs. Middleton, a white lady, residing near Muscogee, and also of being the parties to go to the home of Floyd. Kittrell, some miles distant, where they were compelled to flee at the point of a revolver in the hands of Miss Lena Bowman, two negroes, both giving the name of Perdue, were brought to the city early last night and lodged in the county jail. Both were arested by Deputies Andrews and Bowman near McKinnon's creek, who accompanied Sheriff Van Pelt to the city with the prisoners. There was some excitement on the streets at the time, as the officers also brought in with them Keyser Brown, charged with murder, but the little excitement soon subsided.

CHOKED MRS. MIDDLETON.

Two negroes, it is charged, entered the home of Mrs. Middleton about 9 o'clock Sunday night and one of them grabbed her and tried to choke her down, but with his companion ran when the woman put up a plucky fight and screamed for help. Neighbors ran to aid her and spread the alarm. A search was instituted at once and late yesterday afternoon Deputy Sheriff Andrews arrested E. R. Purdue and another negro of the same name as suspects. Andrews says he carried the negroes before Mrs. Middleton, that she identified E. R. Purdue as the negro who choked her and that Purdue made a break for liberty at once. The officer clubbed the negro with his pistol, cutting his scalp so badly that it had to be sewed when he reached the jail. The other negro was so frightened that he trembled like a leaf and fell inside his cell when he reached the county jail in what is called a jail fit, but recovered afterwards.

A PLUCKY WOMAN.

Before being captured the two negroes went to the place of Floyd Kittell and attempted to come up to the house, but Miss Lena Lowry, daughter of Deputy Sheriff Lowry, grabbed a pistol and drove them away. She then notified her father of what had happened and described the negroes. Mr. Lowry joined Andrews and with him brought the negroes to jail.

Both Andrews and Lowry seemed positive that the right negroes had been captured and Andrews said there was no question as Mrs. Middleton had identified one of the negroes as her assailant.

Mrs. Middleton was not badly injured by the negro who grabbed her, as she fought him so furiously and raised such a cry that it brought help immediately.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A13:
RETURN WITHOUT NEGRO ALLEGED SLAYER KEPT IN PEN- SACOLA PRISON. Sheriff of Baldwin County Fears Trou- ble if Keyser Brown is Tak- en to Scene of Mar- shal's Murder.
Pensacola, Fla., Aug. 23.—(Special)—Taking the advance of Sheriff Van Pelt and Chief of Police Sanders, the thirty or more Baldwin county men, headed by the sheriff of the county, left here today without Keyser Brown, the negro who has admitted that he was one of the two men to commit murder.

The local officers advised against the Baldwin county sheriff's taking the prisoner with him, unless he was looking for a lot of trouble in protecting him, for they were free to say that he would be lynched and probably a number of other lives lost.

They were willing to surrender the prisoner to the sheriff, for it was for him that the officers worked so hard to get the man, but they thought it ill-advised to take him to the scene of the crime with feeling running so high.

The Baldwin Sheriff took that view of the case and with his posse mounted the horses and rode away this morning, intending prosecuting the search for Sydney Hunter, the other negro implicated, before returning to their homes.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A15:
RETURNS FROM HIS VACATION Assistant Postmaster Francis W. Hayes, who has been spending a vacation of two weeks in Michigan, has returned home and resumed his duties at the postoffice. He has much improved by his rest.
Sheriff Van Pelt and Chief Sanders both stayed on duty all night and until daylight this morning following the receiving of a message from a reliable citizen about 7:30 o'clock last night that a mob was organizing at or near Muscogee to come to the city and take from the jail the two Perdues, arrested Monday afternoon on the charge of attempt at criminal assault.

The first precaution taken by the sheriff was to take the two negroes from the jail and carry them in a carriage to a good hiding place. He then returned and strengthened the guard about the jail.

About midnight the information was given the sheriff that a Mobile citizen had remarked in the corridors of the San Carlos that six automobiles had left Bay Minette for Pensacola with five men riding in each machine. That was another thing, for Keyser Brown, the negro who was arrested on the charge of murdering Marshal Smith of Bay Minette, is confined in the county jail. The sheriff decided at once that if he got through the night in safety with his prisoner that he would wire the sheriff of Baldwin county to take charge of the negro.

Occasionally two or three men would come in sight of the jail, linger and in time be told to move on, but up to 3 o'clock no mob had shown up to storm the county bastile.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A17:
S. T. ANDREWS IS DISCHARGED BY THE SHERIFF SHERIFF LEARNED THAT THERE WAS NO TRUTH IN THE STATE- MENTS MADE BY ANDREWS RE- GARDING NEGROES—THE MEN HAD NEVER CONFESSED AND ARE NOT THE RIGHT ONES.
Deputy Sheriff S. T. Andrews, the man who arrested the two Perdue negroes and charged them with criminal assault upon Mrs. Middleton near Muscogee, was yesterday relieved of his commission by Sheriff Van Pelt, the latter writing a letter to the deputy in the morning telling him to send in his commission at once, as he is no longer in the employ of the sheriff.

This action was taken after the sheriff had learned the true state of affairs relating to the arrest of the two negroes, and the manner in which Andrews had treated them. The sheriff was angry when he learned how Andrews had acted, and said that The statements made by the deputy were a tissue of falsehoods. Instead of the two negroes being identified by Mrs. Middleton the latter very emphatically told Andrews the negroes were not the ones. In the face of this, Andrews brought the two negroes to the city, after badly beating up one of them. Upon reaching the county jail he turned to the crowd and informed them for what the negroes were arrested and added: "I'm the bully that can straddle them—they're the right negroes, boys."

CONDITION OF NEGROES.

According to the statement of the sheriff the two Perdue negroes were in no condition to leave the jail yesterday, after the rough handling Andrews gave them and the sheriff said he feared one of them might not leave the jail alive. He says that he told the negroes there was no charge against them and if they were able and wished to do so they could go there own way.

While the jailer and the chief deputy was assuring people about the jail Monday night that the negroes were not the right ones, Andrews was making his way down Palafox street talking with many people, describing their crime and assuring them that he had captured the right negroes and that they had been identified. The action of Andrews at the jail and his subsequent action was taken by many as nothing short of attempt to start a race riot.

keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A20:
FORMER DEPUTY ARRESTED CHARGED WITH MISTREATING TWO NEGRO PRISONERS. Ex-County Official Gives $200 Bond for His Appearance—Negroes Charged With Attempted Criminal Assault.
Pensacola, Fla., Aug. 27.—(Special.)—Former Deputy Sheriff Sim Andrews, who arrested the two Perdue negroes early in the week, charging them with attempted criminal assault, today was himself arrested by the Sheriff on the charge of assaulting the negroes with his revolver. Andrews gave a $200 bond for his appearance.

The father of the negroes is the prosecutor, and it is alleged that Andrews beat the negroes after they had been handcuffed, and also after he had been told by the woman before whom he carried them that they were not the right parties. After this Andrews brought the two men to the city, and when they reached here it is said they were in bad shape, one falling unconscious as he reached the jail.
keyser-brown-muscogee-1910-08-21.A21:
NEGRO TAKEN TO MOBILE WILL NOT BE KEPT IN BAY MINETTE JAIL. Sheriff Booth Brings to Alabama from Pensacola Man Charged With Murder of Marshal Smith.
Mobile, Aug. 27.—(Special.)—Sheriff Booth of Baldwin County arrived in Mobile this afternoon with Kiser Brown, the negro who shot and killed Marshal Smith of Bay Minette several weeks ago.

The negro has been held in jail at Pensacola, and desirous of getting him into the State of Alabama, Sheriff Booth left the Florida city Saturday and came through Bay Minette. At that place and points between there and Mobile, passengers took the train for this city, and when they heard that the murderer of Marshal Smith was on board, held conversations with him.

The negro does not deny he was in the crowd that killed the marshal, but will not say that it was he who fired the fatal shot. The authorities state that Brown was the man who did the killing.

Sheriff Booth was asked to take Brown to the jail at Montgomery, but he said he considered the jail of Mobile County the most convenient, and, for that reason, came here with the prisoner.

Sheriff Booth stated that there is a good clue to the other negro, Sydney Hunter, but did not care to say where he is thought to be hiding. The hunt is being maintained vigorously, and the Baldwin County people are confident of capturing Hunter. Brown is wounded in several places but manages to get along without difficulty. At Dyas, the night after the killing of Marshal Smith, he was shot in the side with a pistol and in the shoulder with a load of buckshot. The jail at Bay Minette is only a frail affair and is some distance from the center of the town and would be easy to enter. For that reason, Brown will be kept here until he is taken back there for trial.

laura-porter-monroe-1910-07-27.A1:
Shame on Louisiana.
Shame on Louisiana. Monroe, La., Special.—Unidentified men broke into the city jail here and carried off Laura Porter, a negro woman prisoner, at whose home white men are reported to have been robbed on several occasions. It is generally believed that she was thrown into the Ouxachita river and drowned.
laura-porter-monroe-1910-07-27.A3:
RACE NEWS
New York, N. Y., July 27, 1910. —Kingsbridge terrace is agog over the selling of a $13,000 house and lot to John M. Royall, a colored real estate dealer. One of the finest on the terrace, the house was owned by Mrs. Sarah Christopher, who lived in it four years. It is a beautiful Queen Anne cottage.

Munroe, La., July 27. Men whose identity the police have failed to establish broke into the jail here today and carried off Laura Porter, a Negro woman prisoner, keeper of a resort where several white men were reported to have been robbed. It is believed she was thrown into the Ouachita river and drowned. The woman had been warned to leave town many times prior to her recent arrest for larceny.

Philadelphia, Pa., July 26. Rev. H. T. Johnson, for a number of years editor of the Christian Recorder, the organ of the A. M. E. church, died here Saturday after an illness lasting two years. The funeral took place at Bethel A. M. E. Church. The services were conducted by Bishop A. Grant, assisted by a number of ministers.

Cambridge, Mass., July 27.—E. Smythe Jones, the Negro poet, who was arrested last week on a charge of vagrancy, after having walked from Natchez, Miss., to this city, in order to enter Harvard this fall, was discharged in the District Court today. Considerable interest has been taken in Jones by the authorities at Harvard, and they have given him employment as a janitor. While in jail here Jones wrote a poem entitled "Harvard Square, and dedicated it to the Judge who dismissed his case.
laura-porter-monroe-1910-07-27.A4:
DIVEKEEPER MAY BE DROWNED Indignant Citizens Believed to Have Thrown Woman Into River.
Monroe, La.—What appears to have been a lynching took place here when Laura Porter, a notorious dive-keeper, was quietly taken from the city jail about midnight by a party of masked men and spirited away. Since then, no trace of the woman has been found.

According to the other women prisoners, she was taken out nude and that an hour later the men returned for her clothing. Just what happened to the woman may never be known, but there seems to be a well-founded belief that she was drowned in the Ouachita river, after having iron weights tied to her. The woman has given the police more trouble than all the other denizens of the tenderloin together. Her most frequent offense was robbing white men, it being charged that she had two or three negro men confederates.

Cries of "Lynch Him."

Cries of "Lynch him!" "Catch the man!" filled the air as several men gave immediate chase. Pedestrians joined in pursuit of the negro, who turned into Twenty-second street.

Led by S. L. Daw, of 1234 Wisconsin avenue, John Linnon, 2223 L street; J. W. Quigley, 2139 Pennsylvania avenue, and Volney Eaton, 2226 N street, the crowd followed the fleeing negro until he turned the corner of L street, where he disappeared in the residence of Mrs. Mary Sanders, his sister.

The crowd burst through the locked door of the shanty.

Search was made from cellar to roof, but without avail. It was then learned that Sanders had made his escape through a rear window into an alley.

Meanwhile the unconscious form of Griffin was taken to the Emergency Hospital. He did not regain consciousness for nearly an hour.

Later he told the details of the assault, saying that the man who had attacked him was Coleman Sanders. He has a police record.

Every Policeman Notified.

Lieut. James Hartley ordered a hunt for the negro, calling out every detective and policeman in the city.

Sanders is twenty-five years old. a mulatto, about five feet nine inches tall. He wore dark clothes. One of his arms is bound in a cloth, having been injured by being hit with a brick.

Griffin, who is thirty-seven years old and lives at Old Dominion Heights, Va., was reported early this morning to be resting comfortably. He will recover, but the surgeons are fearful that blood poisoning will set in.
presley-griffin-washington-1910-08-03.A3:
ASSAULT ON WATCHMAN
PRESLEY GRIFFIN KNOCKED UNCONSCIOUS BY NEGRO.
Assailant Had Been Driven From Park, and Threw Stone in Revenge.
Resenting what he considered unwarranted interference. Coleman Saunders, colored, twenty-five years old, is alleged to have murderously assaulted Park Watchman Presley Griffin in Washington Circle last night about 11:30 o'clock. The watchman was struck by a stone back of his right ear, with force sufficient to knock him down and render him unconscious. A message was sent to the third precinct police station telling of the assault. The patrol wagon was used as an ambulance to hurry the injured man to the Emergency Hospital.

A number of persons were in the park when the stone was thrown. Several started in pursuit of the negro. Saunders outdistanced his pursuers, entered the house of a relative on 26th street and escaped by way of an alley. Policemen from the third precinct and Detective Harry Warren participated in the investigation of the affair, but this morning the man wanted had not been captured.

It is stated that Saunders had been told several times to keep out of the park. It was also said last night that some person, presumably a policeman, had tapped him on his foot to awaken him and that he probably thought Griffin was the man who had disturbed his slumber. He gave the park watchman no opportunity to defend himself, it is declared.

Griffin was unconscious only a short while. At the hospital surgeons dressed the wound. They decided that the skuil was not fractured, and say the patient is on the road to recovery. Griffin is thirty-seven years old and resides at Old Dominion Heights. The police sent a description of Saunders to the several stations last night, with instructions that every effort be made to apprehend him.
presley-griffin-washington-1910-08-03.A4:
Coleman Saunders Captured.
Coleman Saunders, colored, who is alleged to have assaulted Park Watchman Presley Griffin in Washington Circle las night when ordered to stop sleeping on a bench at that place, and who later es caped after an exciting chase with pedes trians, was captured at 2:30 o'clock this afternoon by Capt. Daley and Policemen Sutton and Anderson of the ninth precinct station. The negro was found in the residence at 220 14th street northeast and was sent at once to the ninth precinct station.

presley-griffin-washington-1910-08-03.A7:
SAUNDERS GOES TO JAIL.
Negro Accused of Assaulting Watchman Cannot Furnish Bond.
Charges of assault with a dangerous weapon were filed in the Police Court today against Coleman Saunders, colored, arrested yesterday afternoon in connection with the attack upon Presley Griffin, a park policeman, in Washington Circle Wednesday night. The preliminary hearing was indefinitely continued pending the result of Griffin's injuries. Griffin was struck on the head with a brick by a negro as he tried to drive the latter away from a bench. It was at first thought that the wound would be fatal, as the skull was fractured. In default of bond Saunders was committed to jail.

Shortly after his arrest on 15th street northeast policemen from the third and ninth precinct subjected Saunders to a "sweating."
presley-griffin-washington-1910-08-03.A9:
ADMITS HE.HIT POLICEMAN.
Negro Pleads Guilty to Assault Charge and Goes to Jail.
Admitting his guilt of a charge of hitting Presley Griffin, a park policeman, in the head with a brick last Wednesday night in Washington Circle and inflicting serious injuries, Coleman Saunders, colored, was committed to jail in default of a $2,000 bond, for the action of the grand jury, by Judge Aukam in the Police Court today.

Griffin, his head and face swathed in bandages, Policeman Waters of the third precinct, several policemen from the ninth precinct and two civilians were on hand as witnesses.

Saunders shortly after the assault was arrested in a shanty on 14th street northeast, whence he fled in an attempt to evade capture.

Later in a ninth precinct cell he is alleged to have made a confession, saying he was drunk at the time Griffin was hit.

"I was intoxicated and sleeping on a bench, when the policeman woke me. I was mad and frightened, and hit him before I knew where I was," he is quoted as saying.

Griffin was removed to the Emergency Hospital after being struck. The physicians at first thought he was suffering from a severe fracture of the skull.
